utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon. If I could just raise two very, very brief matters, administrative matters. The first is that, as you'll recall, a number of photographs were taken during the site visit. I may want to use some of those photographs during the cross-examination of Mr. Hansen on Monday. I'm wondering if the Court would give us permission to go to Mr. Lesic, who took the photographs, and obtain the photographs from him so that we could prepare to use them on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The photographs were taken on the instructions of the Trial Chamber. It is the Trial Chamber that has the control of the photographs, and the Trial Chamber will therefore direct that they be made immediately or, at any rate, as soon as possible available to both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm grateful. The second matter is, as Your Honours are in no doubt aware, the parties have filed a combined motion to modify the Scheduling Order. We are in -- we are at the moment planning the final weeks of the trial in terms of witnesses, and so if we -- the sooner we could learn whether we're going to get the four extra days that we've requested for the Prosecution case, the happier we will be and the better we'll be able to plan those last weeks. Because if we do not have that time, we will have to start dropping witnesses, and we need to -- we need to start planning that now. So I just raise that, the urgency of learning that part of the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will give our decision by Tuesday of next week. But you want four extra days, but tell me the effect of the motion would have the Defence open their case how many days beyond the time that the Trial Chamber had set, or weeks?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I have to do the math. We're asking for four extra days, and then we're asking for three additional -- I'm sorry, four additional days of notice. So that is -- we're asking for eight, eight days, and then the Defence, I believe, is asking for an additional 13 days, I believe. And so if you add that up, that is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: About a month?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It ends up being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That the Defence case would start about a month later than the Trial Chamber had envisaged in its order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it's a little bit less than a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: A little less than a month?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, but that's not far from correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At any rate, we'll consider it and give our decision by Monday or Tuesday of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Now, I'll just give a decision. On the 16th of March, the Prosecution filed a motion for testimony to be heard via videolink. This is the testimony of Dr. Sefik Beslic. The Defence did not object. In light of the submissions made by the parties, as well as the law that is applicable, the Chamber orders that Dr. Beslic's testimony be heard via video conference link, and in that regard, the Registry must take all reasonable steps to ensure that the link is established from the Tribunal's Sarajevo's field office during the week of the 2nd to the 5th of April. Now, I turn now to the witness's evidence and to the question which engaged us at the end of yesterday's proceedings. This is a matter that we have been wrestling with for some time. It has to do with the preoccupation of the Defence to lead evidence which relates to activities by the ABiH army, which relates even to violence by the ABiH army without showing how those activities of the ABiH army relate to the issue of liability of the accused. How does it affect the question of criminal liability? And I have been asking Mr. Tapuskovic time and again to explain. On some occasions, I have been satisfied. Yesterday, I asked him again, and I have the transcript here in which Mr. Tapuskovic in answer to my question: Is this related to any of the charges, any of the incidents? And his answer was to say that the intensity of the fighting was such that this was ongoing, and there were casualties on both sides. He went on to say that this shows how many settlements in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps had been captured with fierce fighting and major casualties on both sides. And then I interposed another time, what does it have to do with the charges? And he says: Everything that is a result of the great number of casualties sustained in this area of the 1st Corps and the army of Republika Srpska, all these casualties of the intensive fighting on both sides. At this moment, he says: I am not going to access which side more or which side less, but this was a front line, and from one minute to the other, there were offensive or defence activities going on, and there were casualties sustained by both sides, and the casualties were primarily the result of this offensive action. This is the gist of Mr. Tapuskovic's explanation as to the relevance. The Chamber does not consider that this explanation provides a sufficient basis for the reception of this evidence and need not remind you that the basic evidential rule governing proceedings in this Tribunal is set out in Rule 89(C), which allows the reception of evidence that is relevant and of probative value. You can forget the Latin nomenclatures tu quoque. To my mind, it is really irrelevant. The essential is whether the evidence is relative and probative. If it is, the Chamber will let it in. It seems to the Chamber that merely to say that there was an intensity in the fighting that led to casualties on both sides and that there were offensive or defensive activities going on and that casualties were sustained on both sides is not enough. The Chamber is not satisfied that a link, a sufficient link, has been established between this evidence, which the Defence is seeking to lead, and the issues raised by the indictment. I have said on more than one occasion that this is not a history class. We are not engaged in writing a history of the conflict in which we want to note every and everything that happened. We are dealing with an indictment which has charged specific violations of international humanitarian law and, even more specifically, has identified 23 incidents resulting from sniping and shelling in respect of which it is alleged that there was criminal conduct on the part of the accused. And unless evidence which the Defence seeks to lead or the Prosecution, for that matter, can be tied to the criminal conduct of the accused, whether by way of incriminating him or exonerating him, the Chamber will rule it as irrelevant, and we do so now. We find that this evidence is not relevant, and we'll not allow evidence to be led on this topic. So let us move on from there. Mr. Tapuskovic. Do you have something to say? I hope it is not in relation to the ruling which I just gave, because I want you now to continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour, Judge Robinson. I have nothing to say in relation to what you have said. I have had a sleepless night; I don't think you did. And I understood full well the objection levelled at me by His Honour Judge Harhoff. I will use the time left to me only to try to lead proper evidence. I must admit that what we debated yesterday could, indeed, lead to such a conclusion on your part, and I really do not have any objections in relation to what you have said just now. I would just like to indicate some of the evidence that has to do with what actually happened, 1995. First, I dealt with general orders at that particular time in time. Maybe I could have skipped them altogether, but now I'm going move on to my cross-examination within the time left and, indeed, I will be very direct in respect of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karavelic, I have in front of me DD00-1805. I have a translation which I ensured through sworn court translators. Mr. Karavelic, that is an order of the command of the 12th Division, Sarajevo dated the 4th of July. The document is in e-court, the English version, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honours, it's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see, this is the command of the 12th Division the 4th of July, report on active combat activities. This report is submitted to the command of the 1st Corps. Somebody signed it on behalf of the commander. Please, what it says here is: "With regard to your document such-and-such dated 4th of July, I hereby submit a comprehensive report on combat activities being carried out by the units of the 12th DKOV in the area of the city of Sarajevo. In the period from 15th of June until the 3rd of July, 1995, we operated with all types of weapons and artillery pieces available to us, over VT -- 300 VT of the enemy. Out of the activity carried out over VT, a large number were shot by direct shots. Out of it, 36 VT to p/k was destroyed. VT are bunkers with personnel PAMs, PATs, infantry weapons, preparations, dormitories, et cetera. "In past combat activities, we believe that we killed around 50 Chetniks, and far more were wounded lightly and/or seriously. We believe that in past combat activities, we have destroyed two tanks, a Praga, a Bovor, an armoured vehicle Glosdika," and so on and so forth. I don't have to read out all of it. And, particularly, I would like to draw your attention to what it says at the very end: "We believe that the number of destroyed or damaged VT, combat and non-combat MV, is greater because we acted upon them in conditions of limited visibility at night, so we did not have an opportunity to observe them entirely." Mr. Karavelic, are you familiar with this report? It was sent to the 1st Command; yes or no? I got this from the archive of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Please tell me first whether what it says here is correct? Is this correct, primarily that you operated at night, that you targeted all of these targets at night?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You're not aware of that. But can you tell me whether it is possible that you, as commander of the 1st Corps, do not know about this kind a report, which shows that military positions that are within civilian neighbourhoods are targeted during the night, dormitories?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dormitories are military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please just say yes or no. First of all, tell me, is this a document that can be brought into question in terms of its authenticity, since it was verified by your archives, the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12th Division was one of my divisions. I had three divisions in addition to that, many other independent units. On a daily basis, I would receive 15, 20, 30 reports. Well, multiply that with the number of days in four years. There is not the remotest possibility of me remembering all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, this is a document that speaks of activities from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All divisions engaged in activity and all units every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From Sarajevo that was under the control of the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because not all of Sarajevo in the valley down there was under your control.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand this last part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, tell me, were these activities coming from that part of Sarajevo that was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always part of the units of the 12th Division were outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you, and you have already said this to me and I will repeat, your strategy was that part of these units should get out of Sarajevo and operate from somewhere else, but the majority remained in Sarajevo and engaged in activity as is related in this document; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything specific about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please, I understand why the witness is saying no. But anyway, DD00-1805, could it please be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit, because it is directly related to incidents that occurred in this period of time. This is a report that covers almost 20 days at the time when the incidents occurred; that is to say, in the months of June and July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not going to make any objection on this one, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, on the question of relevance, would you explain the relevance of this to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please look at this. This is June and July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not the period that I'm concerned about. It's the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The time frame, as it says here, is between the 15th of June and the 3rd of July. That is 18 days of daily operations from all kinds of weapons. The 12th Corps was in Sarajevo, and the 12th to the 14th was out of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But what does it have to do with any of the incidents? Does it help to exonerate the accused? Bear in mind, of course, I'm not saying there is any burden on you. The legal burden remains on the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is it possible to endure for 20 days being fired upon without even trying to respond to that? And then, of course, the consequences may be unpleasant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. This is -- this is the rub. You have asked: Is it possible to endure all of that for 20 days without even trying to respond? But you are not saying that that was response -- you're not saying that that response relates to any of the incidents. Your accused, your client, rather, is charged with specific criminal conduct. You're not saying that that response -- if you're saying that that is responsive to -- to particular action by the ABiH and, therefore, the incident charging sniping in respect of, say, incident number 2 or number 3, that that explains that incident. There is no liability on his part. I have to say that I have been through this with you before in another case. It's really a repetition. We're not writing a history. If you can -- if you can say that the response of the Serb army accounted for the death of one of the victims in the sniping or shelling, then of course it is relevant, because they were responding properly to activities or to action taken by the ABiH army. But you haven't said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm telling you please look at this. There was an incident which took place on the 16th of June, actually there were two incidents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's what I want. Let us be specific. What is the incident?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 28th of June. There are numerous incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a second. Incident on the 20th of June. Sniping or shelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assert that there was no intentional engagement of targets, whether they be civilians or anyone else. This was merely something that had to be done and please look at the incidents that took place in this period. It's another matter whether these incidents -- who the perpetrators of these incidents were identified, whether they have been identified or not. But look at the period when these incidents happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the period? What's the period?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The period is as it says here, from the 15th of June until the 3rd of July but it was extended for another month and I'm going to prove that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The 15th of June to the 3rd of July. We have shelling incidents 16th of June, we have three shelling incidents the 16th of June; one on the 18th of June; one on the 28th of June -- two on the 28th of June; and one on the 29th; and two on the 1st of July. Now what you're something is that -- I'm trying to understand how your case is being put. Is that the -- these shelling incidents which allegedly came from Serb fire were merely responsive to some activity on the part of the ABiH. Is that -- is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am even saying that none of these incidents, especially the ones presented so far, did not result from the fire from the Serbian weapons. And that is what I'm claiming. Even in -- if something happened as a result of the use of arms by the VRS, then it would have been something that took place during the BH army's offensive while the Serbian side was compelled to defend itself. Their aim was not to target the civilians or kill the civilians. All these incidents took place during this fiercest offensive during this 20 days and onward throughout the month of July. It has not even been proved that they have been committed by the Serbian side at all. Therefore, the Serbs did not respond in order to retaliate and achieve vengeance it was simply a case of self-defence without desire to kill anyone. They only engaged legitimate targets and those were firing positions that fire was coming from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have a couple of very brief points to make and the first is that I'm a little concerned just about the way the record reads in terms of relevance in connection with specific incidents in the indictment. Of course, we have charged specific incidents, but the indictment is not limited to those specific incidents. Those are representative incidents and we have charge of a campaign of shelling and sniping and a campaign of terror. So I just wouldn't want record to suggest that if a piece of evidence can't be linked to a specific evidence it is therefore irrelevant, and I don't think Your Honours are suggesting that but I just wanted the record to be clear about that. And -- that's actually all I wanted to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That is taken for granted. We will allow this evidence. We will admit the document you're seeking to tender.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will go in as D159.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm only going do deal only with this kind of documents until the conclusion of my cross-examination. Now, let's move to another document, DD00-1799. I also have a translation provided by a sworn in-court interpreter. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is another regular combat report sent to the 1st Corps, and it's yet again signed by the 12th Division commander or someone who signed on his behalf, and it speaks about the 1st of July, 1995. It says the unit is in full combat readiness. The most important artillery operations were carried out against the area of the Nedzarici barracks with 80 and 120-millimetre mortars. Our structure of fire was designed to hamper enemy engineering works. The same purpose was the use of 100-millimetre Howitzer and T55 tanks which was used twice to fire on Gusica Hala. All targets were engaged with high degree of precision. Witness, here we see that mortars were used, 120-millimetre mortars, even a tank was used. Can you confirm that this actually happened and that you knew that a tank was used to fire at Nedzarici; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first part of this document, under item 1, "aggressor", it says two 120-millimetre shells hit the Oslobodenje building at 1125 which signified the beginning of artillery barrage fire on the city. The locations around the Presidency of the republic UN observation post, transit, Jewish Cemetery, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about this. I'm asking you about your actions?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 2 is a direct result of item 1. Anyway, I cannot tell you anything else about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show me where Nedzarici are on this map behind you?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is Nedzarici in the inner city?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please show me on the map?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm now pointing at Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So next to Rajlovo?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's far away from the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like this document also to be tendered and admitted into evidence. I'm not going to comment how come that the witness said no about this document that he has no knowledge, although he was the commander of the 1st Corps, and the 12th Division was part of the corps that he was commander of. Because what I would like to emphasise here under "our forces," it says that fire was intended to hamper engineering work. This is what it literally says. It has nothing to do with the activities of the VRS, but, rather, that these actions were taken in order to make engineering works impossible; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber, it is that questions like this would be the same as if I asked someone what kind of homework you did in the 8th grade in the first week of the second term.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, at this time I don't have a point to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's an issue that affects the trial. You must have a view on it. I don't understand how you can have no view on the admissibility of a document. It's a strange position.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have a view on the admissibility of the document, but I didn't understand that to have been raised at this point as a question or my friend to have made a request to tender the document. I certainly have a view as to the admissibility of the document in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Haven't you? I thought he had asked for it to be admitted. Haven't you asked for it to be admitted, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, especially because of the tank that is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I stand to be corrected. I see it now at the bottom of page 14, Your Honour. I have -- my view about the document, Your Honour, especially in light of the additional information or evidence that Mr. Tapuskovic is offering, is that it should -- is that, first of all, we should be proceeding with a complete translation of the document, rather than an excerpted translation of the document. You've now heard evidence from the witness about a paragraph which you don't see translated in front of you at all, Your Honour. But, secondly, Your Honour, this -- it's not as far away from the story as I've seen it, but the action, the area, the ... What's described in the document is carrying out of a war. It has no relation to the charges at hand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the difficulty that we have is that you seem to be acting as if your client was charged with using armed force, and so you seek to prove that the other side, too, was using armed force against the VRS, but this - at least in my view - is not relevant to the case because I think it is accepted by the Prosecution that there was an armed conflict, and I hope that I'm not saying too much if I say that the Chamber, too, accepts that there was an armed conflict. This is not an issue in this trial. So we don't have to be reassured that both parties were addressing attacks on the other, and that in the course of those attacks both parties suffered a great number of casualties. That's not the issue. The issue is whether some of the crimes, the violations of international humanitarian law that were committed during these attacks, whether those violations were in any way attributable to your client. And, therefore, I wish that we could focus directly on anything that could explain the circumstances and the origin of those crimes, rather than carrying on with looking into evidence about the armed conflict as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, already yesterday I was in a position to make closing arguments in a way without having heard all of the Prosecution case. I have been brought into that position yet again, but the first time I opened this indictment in the general allegations and also in Count 1, the first thing I noticed is that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps carried out a long-lasting campaign of shelling and sniping against the civilian population and civilian areas of Sarajevo, and that that was the only objective that it had. Now that we're talking about these circumstances here from the 12th of August, 1994, until the end of the war, that cannot be said at all. So what I have to do as the Defence, first and foremost, is to deal with the first count, that there was no systematic shelling or sniping at the city, and these documents show precisely what it was that was happening in 1995. Of course, I'm going challenge many other things as Defence counsel with full responsibility regarding these things that were happening in Sarajevo, but it is not my duty to explain that now. At this point in time, on the basis of these documents, it is clear that it is absolutely unacceptable that the first charge from here was present at all; that is to say, the crime of terror described in Count 1 and the Serb side holding the hills around Sarajevo and doing this from there. So that is what Dragomir Milosevic was indicted for, but I think that these documents show that in 1995 there was no such thing. So it is my duty to say today what should be said on another occasion. We see here that a cannon or, rather, a tank is engaging objectives within the city itself, and it should be in the exclusion zone anyway, and now I have to explain whether this is relevant or not; whereas, the accused has to defend himself from charges of having attacked Sarajevo by shelling and sniping. I mean, if I have to deal with that now, it is better for me to sit down and not do anything. If this is not relevant, if this offensive was taking place and if this system -- I mean, this strategy -- I mean, that civilians were targeted mercilessly; I mean, if these documents do not have probative value -- I understood your objection in respect of what was done yesterday, but I obtained 6.000 documents which show activities of the BH army on a day-to-day basis. 6.000, not only of the division but also of the lowest ranking brigade. I have all these documents, but I don't know how to deal with all of them now to show you that there was shooting and action coming from Sarajevo every day. I'm quite serious, 6.000 documents. These are just blatant examples. Let me just say how many weapons were used and even Howitzers, cannons and 152-millimetre guns, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I don't think we will get much further on this line of argument. I think I have made my point clear, and I suggest we move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber, by majority - Judge Harhoff dissenting - will admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become D160.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have two documents related to the same day, the 25th of June, which show the number of shells fired, 120-millimetre shells that is. The document is DD00-1918. I have a translation of this document in its entirety; it's a short document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must be bringing your cross-examination to a close now. I will not allow it go on much longer. You have had your four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes. If necessary, I will complete it right this second, but I explained all these things, and I spent certainly half of my time doing that, in giving those explanations, but all right. It is my duty to answer your questions, and I think it would be only proper to extend my time a little bit more. And I will be very brief with the next witness -- rather, the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The computation of the four hours has not included the time spent in answering the questions raised by the Trial Chamber. Now, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the document is DD00-1918. It's already there, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I really would like the transcript to show just -- to show what I just said, which I consider to be important, which is that the computation of the four hours allocated to Mr. Tapuskovic does not include the time spent by Mr. Tapuskovic answering questions raised by the Trial Chamber. That is important in the interest of fairness to Mr. Tapuskovic that that be understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, Judge Robinson. Can we look at this document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Honourable Witness, again, this has to do with a combat report sent to the command of the 1st Corps, you primarily, dated the 5th of June, 1995. I would just like to show you what it says here: "Our forces. The ammunition used in the afternoon hours ...", and then it says exactly how many mines: 60-millimetre mines, 82-millimetre mines; and over here mortar shells: 120-millimetre, 43 pieces of that in the afternoon. You know that daily, during your offensive, hundreds of shells were fired?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The document doesn't say "shells" anywhere in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it says ammunition used in the afternoon hours on the 25th of June, 1995. Ammunition used in the afternoon hours, and then what the quantity used was for these mortars, 43. In the afternoon, and I have the morning figures as well. The amount is the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't see anywhere in the translation reference to anything to do with mortars, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the English version, Mr. Tapuskovic -- unless it is MB, what does MB stand for? Can the witness tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mortar -- the general abbreviation for mortar is that, except that the calibre has to be added, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Edgerton, Mr. Tapuskovic evidently has more in that art than you do. Let us proceed quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does this report correspond to the actual situation? You received reports every day on the amount of ammunition used, especially in terms of large calibres.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't me. It was my corps command that received these reports. I'm only the commander of the corps, but it is the entire command that commands the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You cannot deny that this is the report sent to you, to your command? You cannot challenge what this document says?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here what the logistic situation was and then what was used up in the afternoon hours. That was used up that afternoon. I don't know from what moment onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber, by majority - Judge Harhoff dissenting - will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D161, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have -- Mr. Tapuskovic, you have five minutes more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then just the document that has to do with the morning, DD00-1991. There is also a translation, English translation of it. Just one more question after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see, this is the document from the same date, but it says in the morning hours. In the time stated here or, rather, combat operations, the following amount was spent. And, again, it says 41 of the 120-millimetre MBs. So on that day, about 100 were used up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before we go any further, I don't think that document was on my list that I was given from the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you really pressing that, Ms. Edgerton? Ms. Edgerton is not pressing that. All right. Yes, let's -- let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is the situation the same like what you said in terms of the previous document?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can barely see anything on this document. I can't read any of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look, it says what was used up on that day. 41, it says.

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see something. It's a poor copy. Now I see it a bit better. The state of logistics; that's what I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just look at 120-millimetres, 41 pieces?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: Shells 120-millimetres 41 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So is that correct at least in this report? Was that used? That's what it says here, used?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like in the case of the previous documents, I cannot confirm that for you, but if this is correct, then that was preparation for preventing the kind of thing that happened in Srebrenica 15 days later, genocide, from happening to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one more document, and then I will finish. For the Prosecutor, it is number 69 on our list.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't heard any request. What did you not object to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also tender this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber by majority - with Judge Harhoff dissenting - admits the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, excuse me, let me just explain that I'm dissenting on the ground that I find these documents to be - as interesting as they are - to be irrelevant to the case, and I would like to add also that my dissent also goes to admission of Exhibit number D159 because that has the same nature. So all four documents are admitted with me dissenting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just this thing and I'm going to finish. That's DD00-1460. I have an official translation provided by the CLSS of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's a letter dated the 4th of April, proposal regarding the extension of the truce, and it's addressed to the President of the Republic, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, and it refers to one of the most important things and that is the truth. I'm going to read only three short passages: "Pursuant to your request regarding the session of the Presidency, I propose the following: An extension of the truce is unacceptable for the following reasons ..." And then the reasons are listed below. And then under item 2: "Demilitarisation of Sarajevo is out of the question for the following reasons ..." And the most thing that I would like to read to you is the paragraph before item 2, which reads: "We must continue saying that we will defend ourselves and that we will not be the first to attack, which is what you always do." Please, this is a letter sent by your commander, Rasim Delic, to Alija Izetbegovic, and it must have certainly be submitted to you as well. You knew this position of the Presidency and your command that truce was out of the question; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is written on paper is one thing and what happened in practice is something completely different.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who is this letter coming from? Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the chief of General Staff, personally addressed to the President of the Presidency with respect to the decision taken by the Supreme Command, and that is what actually happened, there was no truce.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that true, Mr. Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: VAHID KARAVELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me again. Do you know how many truces there were? I can ask a counter-question to you. There were numerous truces, and none of them sustained. It was because of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that all this happened. I didn't have any -- any food. Why didn't they -- why didn't the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps open Sarajevo for just one kilometre?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Witness, this is an interesting comment in the letter. "We must continue saying that we will defend ourselves and that we will not be the first to attack, which is what you always do." That would seem to me to be reflecting a policy position of the -- of the ABiH. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was sentenced to death in Sarajevo. And the whole of Sarajevo was sentenced to death --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I never asked you, never asked you that. Just answer the question. I'm saying that I find very interesting this observation in the letter that it has now gone off the board - here it is - that "We must continue saying that we will defend ourselves, and that we will not be the first to attack ..." I'm saying that that appears to me to be reflecting a policy position on the part of the ABiH. What it seems to me to be saying is that it is placing more importance on a statement as distinct from what might actually be the reality of the situation. It's almost like a public relations statement. Say that we will always defend ourselves, even if that is not actually the position. Say that we will not be the first to attack, even if that is not actually the position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, let me begin with that, even if this is true, as you, Your Honours, have interpreted, the BH army throughout the whole war was by far in a more inferior position with regard to the army of Republika Srpska; it was powerless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said that yesterday and I had wanted to -- to raise that with you. When you say "inferior," not in manpower. Was the BiH army inferior in manpower to the Serb army in terms of the number of forces available to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speaking about inferiority, Your Honours, the first thing that you look at is weapons. Manpower is just cannon fodder. That applies to all the armies. Nowadays the US army can defeat any army with very few number of forces. What matters in a war is equipment and technological development. Nowadays, technology overrides human factors and that applies to specifically to today's state of the art, armament and equipment. A shell can kill 100 people. Human beings are nothing compared to a shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand, you know -- I understand the explanation that you have given. In respect of the -- the question of the inferiority of the BiH army, but I don't believe you have answered or commented on the issue that I raised, that arose from the observation in the letter, that we must continue saying that we will defend ourselves and that we will not be the first to attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to give me a minute or two to give an explanation instead of just saying yes or no. Sarajevo was unable to survive. An army commander was responsible for both Sarajevo and the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We are now talking about Sarajevo. In order to make it possible for Sarajevo to survive, including its population and its army, and to defend itself. Despite many agreements that were never honoured these were just dead letters on paper and they were never honoured by the VRS and it's international community knows that very well. We became indifferent to that. So it's small wonder that the commander wrote this to the President. Mr. President, do politically whatever you want. What we can and must do is to fight in order for us to survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. And I think we have concluded the cross-examination. We'll admit -- do you want to have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit this. We admit this document. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as D163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, that concludes your evidence. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, I see you have been waiting patiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, I have been waiting, Your Honour. Sorry. Your Honours, the Prosecution calls Patrick Van der Weijden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Weijden is called under 65 ter, I believe? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Weijden is an expert, Your Honour, and he will be introducing a report, and then I have some questions about the report. I will take the opportunity of saying that this witness was the subject of some discussion yesterday, and it appeared the cross-examination was running a bit long and that Mr. Tapuskovic did agree that whatever happened, Mr. Van der Weijden could leave today. He is a serving officer in the Dutch army and he needs to be redeployed on Saturday. And I will also tell that my own direct examination will be as brief as possible. The time estimate for the Chamber is one and one half hours, and I can say I certainly will take no more than one hour, and I hope less than even that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, and for please forgive me for failing to remember the character of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit and you may begin, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, would you introduce yourself to Their Honours by telling them your name and also what it is that you do for a living?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: My name is Patrick Van der Weijden. I'm a Dutch army Special Forces Lieutenant. My specialty in the Special Forces has been sniping for, at least, the last 13 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Van der Weijden, how long have you been a member of the Dutch army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I've been a member of the Dutch army since 1990. I have been out of the army on two occasions on one-year breaks, but in all since 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And did you start your career as an enlisted man?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I started my career as an enlisted man, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And then got commissioned as you went along?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you summarize for Their Honours the -- you've mentioned that you are a Special Forces officer and that you specialised in sniping. Could you summarise for Their Honours the - I'll call it - the formation of a sniper in the Dutch army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: My career started in the mechanised infantry, which is infantry that uses army personnel carriers to go into combat and use them as support. That was my initiation in the army. Later when I rejoined the army as a career soldier, my first unit was an airmobile unit in which I served as a sharpshooter, which is an infantry soldier within a regular infantry group who uses a slightly accurised rifle compared to regular soldiers to be able to shoot at longer distances that most other soldiers in his unit. After deployment to Bosnia, I joined up with the army Special Forces to become a -- and in that unit, which is at this time still the only unit in the Dutch army which deploys -- officially deploys snipers, I received sniper training and later also served as a sniping instructor on several occasion and got my sniper instructor degree in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Van der Weijden, did you at the request of the Office of the Prosecutor, prepare a written report for this trial?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And there is a document to your right as you sit there. Is that the report that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: This is a copy of the report I prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Chamber issued an order admitting this report at an earlier date, and at this time I would respectfully ask that an exhibit number be assigned to the report and that it be completely admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours the report becomes Prosecution Exhibit P514.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, the report that Lieutenant Van der Weijden prepared contained the names of several protected witnesses. That document was, therefore, filed under seal. The document that has been uploaded into e-court and that we will be using today is identical, except that those witnesses' names have been changed to their witness numbers. So a number has been replaced with "W-" what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Van der Weijden, were you asked to assess the places from which a shot could have been fired in respect to scheduled sniping incidents in the amended indictment in this case?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Would you please walk Their Honours through the methodology that you used to work out what was the most likely origin of fire in these scheduled incidents.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: At each occasion, I visited the incident site together with the Prosecutor and an investigator on the scene. At every incident site, I looked at the -- the surroundings and tried to determine what is tactically possible for a shot to have originated from. After determining what those possibilities were, I looked at the tactical possibility; for instance, someone -- if there are houses in the area, among the possibilities, but also open fields. An open field will be less likely to have been the point of origin from the shot because it's tactically not wise to stand out in the open on a field for your own safety. After looking at it tactically, well, then, I reached the conclusion what the most likely area was where the shot might have originated from, and I wrote up -- I made my conclusions into a report that I have here on my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant, would I be correct in saying that when you assign an origin of fire in an incident, in your report on the maps, for example, or the photographs that you have marked up, that tends to be an area rather than a specific point?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, it's -- it's time for the break. The legal officer will attend at my chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the delay, for the lateness in starting. We had to be carrying out consultations. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant, just before the break, we had been talking about whether your opinions as to the origin of fire were precise or general, and in connection with that I ask that page 23 of the English version, page 22 of the B/C/S version of your report in e-court be published at this time. And, Lieutenant, I see you going through the report. The page numbers I use will be one higher than the ones on the report -- excuse me, one lower than the ones on the report. I'm sorry, I'm off by one page. On the monitor in front of you, Lieutenant, you see a schematic that you've done, and according to the key in the lower right-hand corner of the colour photograph, the area outlined in red, but white inside, is location of shooter, and obviously that is not a point; it is an area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what I'd like you to do now is just explain to the folks in the courtroom why it is that you are limited to an area as the likely origin of fire, rather than getting it down to a specific point?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The reason why I could not make a pinpoint location is because from -- several locations within the building it was possible to get a view of the incident site, and since I didn't have signs of -- there aren't any signs left now of shooting in the building, there are some bullet-holes visible on the outside of the building where people fired back at the building. There are no shells remaining, there are no shooting positions visible anymore, and so for me it was only possible to get a general location where the shooter might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And continuing on the format of the report, if I could ask the court officer to turn to the next page in both versions. We can proceed because it's the photographs that I'm interested in and not the text. We see at the top of the page on the left a curricular photograph with three blue silhouettes in it; one larger than the other two. And then below that, we see a photograph with some red text on it. The top photograph, with the three blue silhouettes, what is that meant to illustrate in this report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It is meant to illustrate that for identification of which I had a separate appendix, according to my information that I received, the victim was 31 and had a seven-year-old son and a daughter as well. This is to depict just what a shooter must have seen, an adult with a small child, which would indicate non-combatant instead of members of the fighting faction. So it's just to indicate that it's an adult and a small child -- two small childs [sic] in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would like to have you clarify this for me, Lieutenant. The sniper from the position at which he was shooting would have been able to identify the persons as an adult and a small child?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How far would that distance be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, the distance was measured by a laser range-finder, which I had with me at the time, and it was 312 metres, which even with the naked eye on a sunny day would someone -- it would give someone with just the naked eye the possibility to see the difference in height, from which you can conclude it's an adult with a child, instead of two adults or several adults.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And so you make that point, then, to illustrate that even from a greater distance of, say, twice that distance, 600, 700 or even 800 metres, with the benefit of telescopic sight, the -- a sniper would be able to identify a person and determine whether that person was a child or an adult?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There are some -- some indicators that can -- which helps you to discern between civilians or non-combatants and combatants, among which is the difference in height or the comparative height for children. And even at a larger distance, even with cloudy weather, you would still be able to see the difference in height. You wouldn't be able to see colours or maybe hairstyles, but it would give you a very good indication that it's a child with an adult, instead of two combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions to follow up on His Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: First of all, am I correct that this photograph was taken from where you believe the shooter to have been?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: This photograph was taken from a window inside an apartment which I visited in Sarajevo. There are some other possibilities because I was only able to visit one apartment, so -- but this apartment does give a view of the incident site.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And my follow-on question to that is if one goes through this report, was it your methodology to always take a photograph from what you considered to be the likely source of fire towards the -- towards the target?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It is my -- if it's possible, I will have taken a photograph, but sometimes if locations not accessible for me, then I naturally won't be able to provide a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: In addition, His Honour was asking you -- excuse me, in response to a question from Judge Robinson, you said that the comparative height was one indicator that a shooter would have. Are there other indicators that a shooter would have in making the decision, Is this a combatant or a non-combatant? And if the answer to that is yes, could you tell us, please, what some of those indicators are?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The answer is yes. Apart from the comparative side -- comparative height, it would be that non-combatants move differently from -- from combatants. A bundle of wood wouldn't be carried by a combatant out in the open, because if you're, well, at war, and you move from a position to position, you do so as fast as you can and try to make use of the cover that's around you. And it's just contradictory for combatants to move -- to walk on a street with a bundle of wood and just walk plainly in sight of possible positions. Another indicator would be just the colour of clothing, maybe hairstyles, accessories. Like I said, a bundle wood. But a handbag would also be a very good indicator of not being combatants. It's just -- or the absence of weapons. It's just little things that add up to making conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, following on to this point and, first of all, for the record, I'm referring to -- the discussion over the last few minutes has been about photo 1 on e-court page 24 in the English version. You also made an effort in your report, I believe, to identify the weapon that was most likely used in each particular incident, and as with location, could you just take a minute or two and walk us through how you went about making that determination and also how precise you were able to be in that determination?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The methodology that I used was using the information provided to me, which is the summary of the incident. In this case, for case number 5, there were -- there is mention of several shots -- well, several shots with sniper rifle is more difficult, of course, than firing a burst through a machine-gun. The distance of 321 metres is a very real distance when using machine-guns. So the combination of several shots in a short time together with the distance would bring me to the more likely use of a machine-gun over a sniper rifle. And then looking at the existing weapons used in the conflict, I draw my conclusion that it probably would have been a machine-gun or a semi-automatic sniper rifle which would also be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And did you follow that same process with regard to each incident that you examined; looking at the range and the type of shot and how many shots were fired and then drawing some conclusions as to what was the most likely weapon to have been used by the shooter?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, can I -- just for clarification, what you see in photo 1, would that be what a sniper would have seen from that apartment building from which you took the photo through his magnifying telescope on a sniper rifle, or would that be what he could see with the naked eye?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would be what he would be able to see with the naked eye, so not through magnification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you have a comparison with a picture showing what the sniper would have been able to see through his magnifying telescope?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant, let's follow up for a moment or two about the apartment from which this photograph was taken. On e-court page 6 - and that does not need to be published, that's simply a reference for the record - but on e-court page 6 in both English and B/C/S, you talk about using streets as funnels, in the context of urban sniping, to make longer shots possible. Do you know what I'm referring to in your report or would you like to see it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I know what you're referring to. Usually in urban sniping or fighting in urban areas in general, the range is dramatically decreased to a very short range. The average range of infantry combats in built-up areas is almost between 5 to 10 metres because of the streets, room-to-room fighting. A sniper -- sniper shots fired in urban environments can be, in general, 25 to 50 metres, but there are possibilities, as the counsel says. If you look down a street, like the street in case number 5, which shows just -- you look down the street, you have few -- or 300 metres, so the range schematically increases, especially if a sniper or a shooter has his position on an elevated position from which he can look into several streets at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And let's take a look at that street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if I could ask to have published 65 ter number 2825, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant, do you recognise the scene that is on this photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you see a street there that could be used as you have explained to help increase accuracy and range by a sniper in an urban environment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: There's a pen on the right-hand side of the monitor, and the court officer will help you, but I'm going to ask you to outline that street for us, please. Just draw a line, a rectangle, illustrating that street?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That would be the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, you have also mentioned in your testimony that you took the photograph, the circular photograph on e-court page 24, from an apartment in a particular building in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Does that apartment building appear on the photograph that is on the monitor in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Would you please take the pen again and would you mark that apartment building by putting an X through it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That would be the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I offer this photograph as marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P515, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Lieutenant, in your --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I'm finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant, again, I don't need these pages published. But you indicate that you were up in a building in the Grbavica neighbourhood with regard to your discussion of case 1 on page 20 of the English and 18 of the B/C/S; case 5 at page 23 in English, page 22 in B/C/S; case 8, page 26 in English, page 27 in B/C/S; case 13, which is page 29 in English and page 31 in B/C/S; and case 14, which is page 32 in English, page 36 in B/C/S. With regard to all of those, you indicate that you were in a building in Grbavica. Is it the building that is marked with the X?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is the building, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, at this time, if I could refer to Exhibit P00097. This would be an exhibit that was introduced during the testimony of Slavica Livnjak in response the question: Do you see the building known as Metalka on this photograph; and, if so, would you mark it with an X? If we could have Exhibit 97 displayed, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant, a number of these scheduled incidents in case concerned firing upon Sarajevo trams; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Is a tram, in your training and experience in the Dutch Armed Forces, capable -- or well-suited to military uses?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It is a slow-moving -- a relatively slow-moving vehicle. It sticks to fixed tracks so it's not able to deviate from a regular -- normal line of travelling. It's usually brightly coloured, lots of windows and it's not armoured, so it's very unsuitable for technical transporting of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: From the building that is marked with an X on the photograph in front of you, and you see down at the bottom a red squiggle, which is marking some tram tracks, do you have an opinion as to whether a sniper in the X building could tell that he or she was shooting at a tram and not at a military vehicle over that range?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it would be very possible to see that it's a tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant, in your training and in your experience with the Dutch army, have you become familiar with the term "rules of engagement"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Usher, we are finished with the SMART Board, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: What does "rules of engagement" mean, Lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The rules of engagement for me mean the guidelines for the use of force that can be used by military units in conflicts or peace-keeping operations. They describe in general when and how force might be applied. In general, for the Dutch army it has always been use force only as -- only if necessary. In peace -- sorry, in peace-keeping operations, force is only allowed to be used for self-defence, and the defence of colleagues or the defence of innocent civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what is the training in the Dutch Armed Forces regarding the legitimacy of shooting at civilians whom you know to be civilians?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: In -- well, what normally -- what usually happens if an incident like that would occur is that the soldier shooting the civilian would be inquired [sic]. If there is a suspicion that he was wrong, he would be arrested, brought to the Netherlands, and put on trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in your experience with the Dutch army, have you worked with armies of other NATO countries?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And based upon what is what you just described as the enforcement mechanism in the Dutch army also generally applicable in other NATO armies?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have two last questions, and then I'll be finished. First of all, in all of the incidents that you reviewed, did you consider the possibility that the shots that struck the person had come from territory under the control of the army of Bosnia and Hercegovina, rather than territory under the control of the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I have not looked at the possibility. For me, it was just purely a theoretical possibility where the shots might have originated from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you concern yourself with who controlled the territory in question, or did you simply refer to the territory itself without regard to which army controlled it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Just the territory itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. Lastly, you have done a report that includes all of the scheduled sniping incidents attached to the amended indictment. In how many of the cases that you examined did you find that a shooter would not have been able to distinguish a civilian from a combatant when he or she took the shot?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I have to add something to that, because at very long distances, of which some of the incidents involved longer distances, it is very difficult to discern between civilian or non-combatants and combatants but again with rules of engagement, it is only after positive identification that are you allowed to take -- to take a shot. So even at the longer ranges where it's very difficult to discern between combatants and non-combatants, I drew the conclusion that fire should have been withheld.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea of what that distance is, the longer distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the distances would be above 6 to 800 metres under cloudy conditions, because weather conditions influence greatly the possibility to identify persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so if a shooter in an army is in doubt about whether the person in the cross-hairs is a civilian or a combatant, what is that soldier to do?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Withhold fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. That concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Van der Weijden, I am Defence counsel for General Dragomir Milosevic, and I would just like to clarify a few matters. First of all, in relation to your profession, as far as I can see from this document, which is basically your professional CV, as far as I can see, you were born in 1971; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when this conflict started in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were 21, 22?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I was 23, 24, and later on 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As I can see from your CV, you graduated from a technical college. You actually have a degree in architecture. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here, it says civilian education: Technical University, Delft, Architecture.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But I don't have a degree. I attended for one year, and then I left the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you were a sniper instructor in 2004; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes. I have been instructing sniping before that, but my diploma or certificate was handed to me in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, basically, you were an instructor for the use of fire-arms; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I still am.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, as I can see, in 2002, you were leader of a team of the 105th Commando Company in Afghanistan? In 2002?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I was -- I became team leader in 105 Commando Corps Company in 2002, but I was deployed to Afghanistan in 2003, in the summer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you actually functioned within a commando group in combat operations; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, I see that your hobbies include military history, walking, and work-related shooting; right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Weijden, you -- you do not have any training in terms of ballistics expertise in the actual sense of the word. You do not have the training that a ballistics expert should have.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I have had some of the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But not of an expert nature, certainly.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I don't have a degree in ballistics, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that the same goes as far as forensic principles are concerned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Particularly, as far as any kind of medical training and education are concerned.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I did receive medical training concerning gun-shots as part of the military, and I did have lessons in [indiscernible] or wound ballistics in several of the courses that I attended, but I don't have a degree in medical science, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, as for this work that you carried out and the findings and the opinion that you gave, can we say, for example, judging by what I saw from your findings, that not in a single case did you bear in mind where the separation line was between the two conflicting parties in concrete situations related to individual incidents?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct. I did not take into account the conflicting lines. The separation line, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Further on can we take this as a fact, and you will say yes or no to that, that you did not take that into account, especially as far as machine-gun fire was concerned, then automatic weapons, infantry weapons and ordinary rifle fire? Not in a single case did you take into account whether the incident occurred close to the separation line or not?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Since I don't know where the separations line were, I wouldn't be able to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: For example, as far as Spicasta Stijena is concerned. You never took into account anything else except for the distance involved. You were proceeding from the fact that the sniper was at a particular location, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: As for Spicasta Stijena, I took into account where the witness -- where the victims say the fire originated from and then I looked, according to my methodology, what is technically possible and then what is tactically a wise position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say, Mr. Van der Weijden, that not in a single case did you establish what the axis of the exit/entry wounds was in terms of the medical documentation? You did not establish where the bullet had hit the body of a person who had lost his or her life, or where the bullet exited from the -- that person's body? I didn't see information of that kind anywhere in your analysis.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct, because I didn't have the medical information available to me, apart from the information in the summary of the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And if you had had that information, would you have been able to establish those things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be difficult to establish those things after a long time like this, but it would help in narrowing down the choice of -- the possibility of which weapon was used and perhaps also in the direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
