utterances.text: Do you know at least that in the case of any killing in principle, we're not talking about the matters involved here, the first thing that has to be dealt with in terms of where a person fired from is very important, because this is one of the most reliable ways of ascertaining where a bullet had come from; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: If you are talking about the medical information, that would be -- it would be very important, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing that I'd like to ask you about: Where you established that an M76 or an M91 using 7.62-millimetre ammunition and 55 er [as interpreted] with optical sights, even where you established that that was the case, you did not establish whether the calibre of that kind of a sniper rifle corresponds to the appropriate medical document; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No. There was no way for me conclude specifically which ammunition was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you do know that sniper bullets fired from sniper weapons have certain characteristics that considerably differ from the characteristics of these other types of automatic weapons: infantry weapons, automatic rifles, that the bullet there is different; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, it's not that different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about your general views pertaining to your findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's document 65 ter 3055, page 3 in English and also page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's toward the bottom of the page where you talk about a sniper and when it became a popular term used in the media and it's still widely in the use. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "It got a new impulse in the conflict in the Balkans. 'Sniper Alley' in Sarajevo is known to the whole world." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you read about this "Sniper Alley"? You read about it at the time when you were much younger than are you now; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you already formed an opinion already back then with relation to this whole issue, which was generally known around the world as the "Sniper Alley"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you reach this conclusion that since that conflict, the world "sniper" is used to indicate a shooter who shoots at whoever he gets in his sights: men, women or children, combatant or non-combatants? Did this belief of yours originate at that period, or how did you arrive at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I arrived at that conclusion even nowadays -- well, the Balkan conflict has been -- doesn't exist anymore. The Iraq conflict still does exist and in that conflict, again, there -- the term "sniper" has been used extensively in the media. So it's every time there's a conflict and civilians are fired upon by people from a concealed position. Time and time again the term "sniper" pops or comes back to be used in the media. I never conclude it is a sniper that is shooting but it's the general opinion of the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Weijden, concerning the opinions propagated by the media, and the fact that it still prevails today that a sniper shoots at everyone regardless of that being a man, women or children, combatants or non-combatants, you think that this applies solely to the Serbian side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring primarily to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you say about this conflict that the same applied to both sides and that precisely on this "Sniper Alley," it sometimes happened that people got shot by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has set out in his report and has testified about the facts that were available to him when he was doing this report. He has testified that he looked at what was theoretically possible in terms of shooting and then narrowed that down but what he understand as a professional soldier to be tactically wise or likely. Nowhere was it mentioned that Lieutenant Van der Weijden has detailed knowledge of operations inside Sarajevo, and I don't understand that there is a basis, therefore, for putting that question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's outside the scope of the report. Ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do my best to finalise this quickly. Let us move on now to page 6 in the English version and also page 6 in the B/C/S version. It's this chapter called "Sniping in Urban Areas," and in paragraph 2 it says: "Large buildings or factories offer multiple possibilities to establish a shooting position."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: In urban areas, were there any high-rise and big buildings that were situated on both sides; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: There are high buildings on both sides, yes. Or, yeah, at least that are high buildings, because I don't know exactly where the -- the line -- the separating line was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same chapter, speaking about the range, you say that: "In built-up areas, shooting ranges are at an average of 75 metres. Long shots are possible only from dominating positions with an overview from above (hilly areas)." Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know at all who was holding these hilly areas primarily; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I know in general who was holding the areas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: According to the media, it was the Serbs that held the mountains around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we discuss a few incidents that you gave your opinions about; for instance, incident -- or case 2 of 24th of October, 1994. It's on page 11 of the English version, and also page 11 in the B/C/S version. This is an incident in which a young boy was hit through a passage, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As Mr. Dragomir Milosevic's Defence counsel, I'm interested in what is actually described on the next page as kind of additional information. You can see it here, additional information, you speak about the distance and then a little bit further on, you said: "The victim cannot have been shot from another direction than the red area in the layout." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That was my conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But then, in the very next sentence, you say: "Only a few possibilities remain where the shooter may have had his shooting position." Is that correct? This is also what you said?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it means that there were other possibilities for someone else to have been shooting at this particular person?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, there isn't. As I have written in the report, the victim -- the possibilities lie within the red area in the layout.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You claim in your report, and on the basis of the photograph here, is that the victim was turned with his chest towards the direction from which the shot had come?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me anything at all about the elevation from which it was possible to shoot at a person who was at the other side of the passage, on the ground? Was that feasible and possible at all, to shoot from a roof through a passage at a person who was on the ground, at the ground level? At the street level?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes. In this case, it was very possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How can you explain that? I read this, but for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, could you please elaborate on this.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: For that, I would need a piece of paper so I can draw something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness have a piece of paper so he can draw something, and then we can look at it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If this were to be a rifle with a scope, when firing a scoped rifle or any rifle, in fact, in general, there are sights on it that can be -- usually can be adjusted to the range. The sight line towards the target will always be a straight line. The longer the distance, the more -- if this were a scope on a long range, this would not be the case but just to get a general impression, the bullet would go up and travel above the sideline to the target and meet up at one distance. At a very long range, which is then I'm talking about above 600 metre, this is distance would be -- could become more than a metre, more than one metre. So it really travels above this in the line of sight. So with that very long distance if a shooter -- a rifleman is here with his rifle and there's a tunnel and his target would be -- would be here, if it's a very long distance, it could happen that a bullet would -- he would be able to see the victim or his target, but the bullet would strike the upper part of the tunnel, so the roof of the tunnel. But at this distance at 320 metres, it would not be the case. It would only be not possible for the shooter not to see the victim if the shooter would be in a very tall apartment building. The tunnel would be somewhere here, and the target would be here. If it's like this, he wouldn't be able to see the target. But at 320 metres, it is very feasible to see the target and be able to take a shot at the target without the bullet striking the roof of the tunnel. I hope this is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. What you draw here is almost a straight line between the passage and the weapon from which it was fired. As I can see here, this line is almost at the ground level. But according to what we heard before, the shot came from a roof of a building. This is what I'm asking you: How is it possible to fire 3 or 4 metres above ground or even more, let's assume that, to hit a person at the other side of this passage?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, as I tried to explain, it has to do with the difference in altitude or the elevation. If the shooter is at very high elevation compared to the victim or to the target, he won't be able to -- he might be able to see the target but not be able to shoot at the target because the bullet will travel above the line of sight and only meet up with the line of sight at the target. So -- but in this case, I strongly disagree with that because at 321 metres, it would probably be -- even if the shooter would be 50 metres above ground level, he would still be able to see and shoot at the target without the bullet striking the roof of building through which the tunnel goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What would be the deviation at the broadest part? Did you say that it is above 1 metre at 600 metres distance; then at 320 metres, what would be the maximum deviation between the line of sight and the ballistic trajectory of the bullet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to get the exact data out of my head, but I believe that with 7.62 times 51 millimetres, which is a NATO -- standard NATO rifle round, if a regular assault rifle is sighted at 300 metres, the bullet will travel not higher than 20 centimetres above the line of sight. So that's only 20 centimetres, which is -- yeah, roughly this distance. To that, I would have to add that the rounds, which I believe were most likely used in this case, which is the 7th -- 762 times 54, which is the round that is used in the M76 but also in the M84 machine-gun, and 7 times 92 times 57, which is a round that is also used -- which are also models available in the M76 and is also used in the M53 machine-gun, and those rounds have slightly similar trajectory characteristics compared to the NATO round. So it's not that much difference -- difference in height.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Witness, please, did you measure the distance of this tunnel or passage, whatever you wish to call it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The distance of the tunnel itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I did not. But my guess would be not more than 10 metres in that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So how could you establish anything at all if you didn't measure the length of the passage precisely? Can you please first make a drawing of this tunnel as you did so in this lower sketch. Was it possible at all to establish anything with respect to someone several metres above the ground and to determine how it was possible for this person to hit someone else through the tunnel at the end of the tunnel? How can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, this would be a roughly because I don't have a centimetre, but it's -- if this would be 300 metres, which I -- 320 metres, so roughly this would be -- divide it into 100-metre sections. Well, then 100 divided into 50, this would be the length of -- approximately the length of the tunnel. So even at that range, it's a very short distance for the -- for the bullet trajectory for which -- when it flies through the tunnel. So the highest -- the culmination point, which is called -- from -- at which -- that's the height at which the bullet is the highest above the line of sight, if that is with this -- with the calibres used approximately 20 centimetres. When it reaches the end of its trajectory before hitting the target, it will drop again to zero, because at 320 metres it will coincide again with the line of sight and be the same as the line of sight. So at the end, it will not be 20 centimetres higher than the line of sight but maybe 2 or 3 centimetres higher. So there's no reason -- it's not difficult or it's not impossible to shoot through a tunnel and hit someone on the other side of the tunnel. It's very possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Witness, that's not what I doubt, but you again drew a horizontal line as the line of the passage of the bullet through this tunnel. There's a difference between these two evaluation. If the point at the top vertically is the point from which the bullet came, how could it have passed through a tunnel which was 10 to 12 metres long and hit someone standing at the other end? Can you demonstrate to the Trial Chamber whether this was physically possible to shoot from this point that you just indicated and for the bullet to pass through a 12-metre long tunnel and hit someone standing at the other end? Not like this, as a straight line. It makes sense. But to shoot from the roof of a building, 300 metres away through the passage, explain to me where is the logic of that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I will try to explain. As I roughly sketched here, this is 300 metres. You would have to agree that a normal building, a two-level building with an attic would not be higher than 20 metres. Do you agree? This is 100 metres, this is 50 metres, so this would be the height at which the shooter would have been, because that was the highest building within the red area marked on my layout. So 20 metres of height, a straight line, it's not that far above ground level. If the building in which a shooter could have been would have been 10 metres in front of the building, then he would have difficulties seeing the target. But at 300 metres at a height of 20 metres, there is no difficulty in seeing and taking a shot at the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I will end with this by stating something like this: First of all, you don't have the exact position from which the shot came, with respect to the height. You did not measure the height between the ground level and the point from which the shot came; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also don't have the exact length of the passage; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I don't have the exact length -- exact length to within 10 metres deviation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You also don't have the exact distance between the passage and the place where the victim was?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I don't have the exact distance, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So how can you make any categorical claims based on which the Trial Chamber can reach conclusions that something really happened without any shadow of a doubt, if you fail to make exact measurements and to give your opinion based on that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The reason why I didn't make any calculated -- or I didn't calculate any data and use that in conclusions because -- because at the time of visiting, there was in my professional view not a doubt that the shooter would have been able to fire from the location that I marked in the layout towards the incident site with a rifle. There would be no problem for -- so it was, for me, beyond a doubt that it would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you have been chosen as an expert to present to us all the data on the basis of which the Trial Chamber can reach a solid conclusion that this is what definitely happened. You did not do what an expert is expected to do in order for us to have a clear picture. You just proceeded from your own beliefs. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I did not proceed from my own beliefs. I proceed from my own personal experience and long shooting experience. They are not assumptions; they are conclusions from my personal experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me why didn't you address this issue in a precise way and proper way? You failed to do that. You went there on the spot, and you were there for -- supposed to establish elementary information in order to make any views or any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have asked too many questions. Mr. Docherty, what --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have two objections, Your Honour. First of all, I object to this as being repetitive. The witness has been asked the same question multiple times. I also object to the immediately preceding question or questions on the grounds that it is compound. There are several questions there, and it's anybody guess which one the witness is to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. Reformulate a single question for the witness, and let it not be a question that you have already asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You did not even climb up to a location from where the shooting perhaps came?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that incident, I have no further questions. Let us move on to incident number 1 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to get a few moments of precision here. This is not the first time that we see each other, so before anything else I would like to greet you and remind that we saw each other in another case three days ago, another case I'm sitting in, and I know you're here in your field of experience. And so the question I would like to ask you is to know whether for this particular incident, when we look at your sketch, is it possible that apart from the point from which the shot originated, there might be another point of origin? Because when you look at the sketch, at the back, or, rather, at the -- the furthest corner on the right there is the target and when we look at the origin of the firing there's an opening, an open angle. You said that you did not visit the site but you said that based on your experience there was not a shadow of doubt as to the origin of the shooting. Could you explain this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to, Your Honour. From what is visible in the layout of -- just the enlarged section of the geographical map, there are other possible fields of fire which would come from the south, the east, or the north. The reasons why I didn't conclude that it had come from that direction is the boy was moving alongside the building towards the south with his friends. The other positions would offer -- they would offer views of the boys and, in my professional opinion, if targets would walk that direction, it would be tactically very -- not -- it would not be smart to start firing when there would be an avenue of escape for the -- for the targets. Because if the shooter would have been in the south, the north, or the east where he would have a view of the targets, the targets at the time the target was shot, the other targets could have -- might have got away through the tunnel to the other side of the building, would be safe for those -- the shooters in those locations. Apart from that, it was also strange that the other boys then were not targeted by the same shooter. The reason why I reached the conclusion that it would have come from that direction is that the boy was only visible to the shooter at that -- at that location and exactly at that location was fired at. So that -- that, for me, that narrows down the possibilities of the location of the shooter. From the position of the blue dot, which marks the location of the victim in the layout, the three buildings, they would offer -- offer a view of the position of the victim. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I just take you back to a question asked by Mr. Tapuskovic when he said that you didn't even climb up to the location where the shots, perhaps, came from, and you said no. Does that mean that if you were told that the shots allegedly came from the sixth floor -- let us say the sixth floor of a building, you did not go to the sixth floor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason why I didn't go into -- go to the building, because at the time -- at the location of the victim, there was -- for me, there was absolutely no doubt that the shots would have come from those buildings. If there was any doubt, I would have gone to the buildings, go up to several of the rooms to try and look at the possibilities. But for me, it was just very obvious that through the tunnel, which -- which they ever -- saying with lasers is lasers point back to you, and same goes for a tunnel. If you're shot through a tunnel, if you look back through the tunnel, that's where the origin of fire will be because bullets still don't -- they deviate and they follow a trajectory, but they still don't go around corners. So it just points back to the location of the shooter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So in relation to this boy who was shot through the tunnel, have you estimated at what height the shooter would have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I estimated the height. I didn't include it into the report but looking at the buildings that were visible through the tunnel, the maximum height of the -- of the buildings would be 20, 25 metres high -- of height, and that would be -- offer no difficulties for the shooter to shoot at the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's time for one more question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back again to what I asked you in the beginning. This time you did not have any insight whatsoever into the medical documentation involved on the basis of which you could establish how a person had been hit, where a bullet entered one's body, and where it exited the body. You didn't even look at that in order to reach a proper conclusion, in addition to all of the other omissions you made?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't look at the medical information, apart from the information available to me in the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As for incident number 18, I don't really want to deal with that, because a witness who was supposed to be heard hasn't been heard yet so I cannot deal with that at this point in time? Honourable Witness, then I would like to you asking about incident number 1, the 8th October, 1994. It's page 18 in B/C/S and page 18 in the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Before Mr. Tapuskovic puts his question could the sketches that the witness has made be introduced into evidence. If Mr. Tapuskovic is not going to move their admission, I respectfully will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that exhibit will be admitted as P516.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Van der Weijden, I would like to proceed from the point where you talk about the calibre of the weapon. You concluded here that most probably automatic rifles fired. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Automatic machine-guns, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that this excludes the M76 and M91 semi-automatic rifle; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then at the next paragraph, you said the M70 assault rifle series have a capability to fire on automatic but are prone to muzzle climb and, therefore, extremely difficult to keep aimed at a target even at ranges under 50 metres; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We said that you did not take into account the separation line that existed, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you say here: "The weapons used will have been the M84 such-and-such calibre or M53 machine-gun Mauser on bipod or tripod mounted? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you say, generally speaking, how you came to this, that this weapon was on a bipod or a tripod at the separation line. On the basis of what information did you come to that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The information is from my personal experience that while machine-guns generally are used on a bipod, on a bipod they are less efficient then when employed on a tripod, especially weighted down with sandbags. Machine-gun on a bipod will, similarly to the M70 assault rifle, have more muzzle climb and move away from the target the longer the burst of target is, but if a machine-gun is mounted on a bipod or a tripod -- or sorry, on a tripod, the efficiency of the machine-gun will go up greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, until now, in these proceedings I did not hear from a single witness that it was established through any evidence that this -- what you have been saying is the case. So this is your assumption, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The basis of an expert's opinion can be drawn from personal experience from training. It does not need to be drawn from what other witnesses have testified to. If that was the rule, no witness could ever say anything original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question that was asked was so "until now in these proceedings, I did not hear from a single witness that" it was established through any evidence, et cetera et cetera. Yes, it doesn't have to be established through evidence, Mr. Tapuskovic. And I'm sure you know that. He gives the evidence on the basis expertise. In fact he is not here as a fact witness. He is here as an expert. So proceed to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was not what I wanted to ask, but I was compelled to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you say that you know this from your own experience that means that when you were a member of those units where you took part in certain actions, you would always put a machine-gun or a rifle on a tripod. Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of what are you asserting now in proceedings like these if you don't even know that from your own personal experience?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The reason to put a machine-gun up on a tripod has to do with several facts. If I carry a machine-gun into battle, it will be -- a machine-gun is not a light weapon, it's over 10 kilos, and over long distance it can be very heavy. So in offensive operations where people move on foot, it's generally used on a bipod because that's the easier way to use it. In set-up positions, such as along separation lines, it is very common for machine-guns to be put on tripods and weighted down with sandbags to improve the efficiency of the machine-gun. That is the reason why I included the part about the tripod.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you said that assault rifles from the M76 series are prone to muzzle climb and, therefore, extremely difficult to keep aimed at a target even at ranges under 50 metres. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Assault rifles from the M70 series are prone to muzzle climb when fired on automatic, not on semi-automatic. So when firing in bursts, it's very difficult to keep on target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand the "climb". Did you say "muzzle climb"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the muzzle. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Muzzle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muzzle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muzzle climb -- when firing a weapon, with the action of the weapon, when the bullet leaves the barrel, there are several moving -- there are moving parts that push the rifle back into your shoulder, but also when the bullet leaves the barrel, the general direction of the rifle to climb is upwards with -- it can be compensated with the use of flash-hiders or with compensators, in which the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: With the use of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of compensators, and with compensators is a device mounted on the end of a barrel that directs the gas in the opposite direction of muzzle climb to keep the rifle more on its target. That is not always present on rifles. And with the M70 series, it is not -- there are versions with have -- which have sort of a compensator, but that's the reason why with assault rifles in general it's very difficult on automatic -- on automatic to keep a rifle on its target instead of it moving away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is not only that you don't know where the separation line was, but you also didn't know that in that part of town where the separation line was, where all these things happened, that the front lines of both sides were barely 15 metres away, and sometimes the front line went through a single house. You don't even know about that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I have read about it in general, but I don't know about the specific incidents, if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Under such circumstances, could anybody have been fixed to a tripod; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting to you -- putting it to you that it is far more logical that no one would dare use a tripod but on the contrary because the warring parties were so close to each other, everyone had to be on the move all the time; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But I am asserting the exact opposite, that everyone had to be on the move, and that there always had to be this muzzle climb; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, I would like to put something directly to you; namely, that in that case, precision could not have been attained even at 50-metre ranges?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Could you rephrase the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask even more directly. Does this mean that under such circumstances, actually, there could only be an exchange of gun-fire, and in that situation there would invariably be this muzzle climb, which would prevent precise targeting and precise hits?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why? I'm asking to you explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In urban warfare, the separation or front lines are usually fluid. They -- one day a house is in a position of one party; next day it can be in the position of the other party. But there are always features in the terrain which are dominated by one party for a longer period of time. And especially with sniping as I have written in the introduction to sniping, the sniper or the shooter, you don't -- the front line is not a straight line; it moves -- it -- it flows through the -- through the terrain according to the positions available or the features in the terrain such as buildings. So it's not a straight line going through all the buildings, which also means that a shooter doesn't have to be exactly on the front line; he could be 100 metres behind the front line and still fire across the front line to the other -- to the other side. So there is -- although most things in urban warfare are fluid, it doesn't mean that there is -- that there are no fixed positions. In addition to that, with the muzzle climb the only -- the weapons that I've -- of which I write about as to being very prone to muzzle climb are the M70 series assault rifles, and those especially I rule out as a possibility. So I didn't because -- because of muzzle climb and their lack of accuracy. So those are the weapons that I've excluded as being -- of being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you in possession of information as to the kind of rifles that would have been used by snipers in conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the -- yes, sorry. The rifles used by snipers in the conflict, they probably would have been used by -- by all sides because the M76 and M91 or Dragunov, which is a copy of a -- a Russian sniper rifle, they were present in large quantities at the beginning of the conflict. So with the conflict, probably all sides would have used the same weapons. But the sniper rifles used in the conflict -- well, M76 and M91, those are the sniper rifles that were used by the military at the time, but there were rifles which were considered obsolete at the time, which was the M48, which was a German rifle in the Second World War, which was also used by Yugoslavia after the war. And in addition, there are also hunting rifles, which would -- could be used but of the hunting rifles, there are such a large variety that it would be difficult to -- to point out a single rifle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But those -- the rifles that you have identified as having been used in the conflict, would they have been susceptible to this muzzle climb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sniper rifles, in general, are optimised for accuracy and will have less muzzle climb than other rifles. The main reason for muzzle climb is firing several shots in a rapid succession, so on automatic rifles tend -- the most impact of muzzle climb, sniper rifles -- there are -- to my knowledge, there are no automatic sniper rifles, there are semi-automatic sniper rifles, but even with those the shooter decides himself how rapidly he fires. And with two -- in my opinion, a shooter with a scope rifle will never fire more rapidly than he would be able to get his scope back on the target again. So with sniper rifles, the muzzle climb is not normal. It happens, but it's not of an impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, if I understand you correctly, what you're saying is that if you have evidence of automatic shooting that does not appear to have been deviated by muzzle, then that shooting most likely would have come from a machine-gun mounted on a tripod; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I have written for this case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But if it is not on a tripod, this M70 weapon and the other weapon, the machine-gun, then it's not a sniper any longer. If it's not on a tripod, it cannot be a sniper rifle anymore. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: For the -- the M70 is an assault rifle which is not possible -- it's not made to be mounted on a tripod. It doesn't have holes in it that are used to put it on a tripod. It's a standard assault rifle similar to the AK47 Kalashnikov assault rifle used by the Russians. The M70 is a Yugoslavian copy of -- of that rifle. I never, in the report, wrote that the shooter has been a sniper, I -- because if someone uses a machine-gun, well, he's not a trained sniper but just a trained soldier with a machine-gun. So there's never a conclusion that it has been a sniper, it has always been a shooter. And from the information I concluded -- from the information provided to me, I concluded what type of weapon was most likely used, and if it was a machine-gun it will not have been a sniper using the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, I have to insist, sir, on this assault rifle, which is characteristic for trench position, it could not have been accurate even at 50 metres with regard and due to this muzzle climb that exists when fired?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I wrote that it is not accurate on automatic. The rifle is more precise when used in a semi-automatic mode, which is every time you pull the trigger, one shot -- one bullet leaves the barrel. You have to release the trigger and press the trigger again to shoot another -- to get another bullet out of the barrel. In addition to the muzzle climb in the M70 series, the sights on the M70 assault rifle are -- have a very short sight radius, which means that the front side and the rear side are a very short distance apart from each other, and it is very similar to air rifle sights and not suitable for shooting at distances over 2000 metres. It doesn't mean that someone won't be able to fire in that direction and or that he will never hit a target over 200 metres, it is just not suited at distances over 200 metre -- 200 metres. But on an automatic, it's a different -- it's different because then the muzzle climb will be -- will force the weapon to -- away from -- from the target and make it very difficult to hit something with -- on automatic distances over 50 metres for a longer time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then, at least, conclude that the use of this rifle is characteristic for an exchange of fire between the parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, I believe this is the rifle that was mostly used by most warriors in the conflict, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During the exchange of fire, when both sides are firing at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I object to the supposition that is contained in that question. There is no way that you can conclude from the type of weapon used that someone is shooting back at you. All that the Lieutenant has done is say this is the sort of weapon that was used to fire a shot. From that, it is impossible to conclude that because this particular weapon was used, someone must have fired back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us hear whether the Lieutenant can answer the question on the basis of his expertise. Are you in a position to answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it wouldn't be yes or no. Well, if there's an exchange of fire in modern conflict, there is no -- no one uses the same -- not everybody uses the same weapon. In every infantry unit there is a mix of machine-guns, pistols, rifles, assault rifles. So it's always a mix of weapons that is used. It's not just the M70 assault rifle, which was the weapon most present on the battlefield properly because it's produced in the largest numbers. But in addition to that, the M84, the M53 machine-guns, the M76, the M91, will all have been used at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You included precisely this rifle in your report as a suggestion, not as a supposition. I would just like to put it to you that given that you said that this particular rifle was used, that it did not allow for precision fire, and I'm asking you wasn't that precisely the rifle that was used on the separation line for -- for returning the fire? I'm not now raising the question who fired first.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Well, most of the warriors on the -- at the separation line will probably have used his rifle, but it wasn't the only rifle used at the separation line, because it's always a mix of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I must ask you again, you yourself said that under such circumstances, this rifle is ineffective. It cannot precisely engage a target, not even at 50 metres. That's what you said. Then this is what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: In this case in which the victims and witnesses mention bursts of fire like a machine-gun, the reason why I included the M70 series of assault rifle is because it is capable of firing automatic, but because of the lack of accuracy at ranges over 50 metres, I ruled it out of the -- as a possibility. It also means that it's not -- in my opinion, it's not a regular line soldier who has fired the shots at the target but a machine-gun mounted on a tripod.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know at all that the army of Republika Srpska has this kind of machine-gun? Do you know that at all?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The machine-guns are still in service and still being produced at the Sastav [phoen] Arms Factory. So I -- I do believe the machine-guns at that time were already in service as well as visualised by the media, and there will be photos newspapers from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can understand, you persistently base your claims on what you heard from the media. I'm asking you, did you have any way at the time when you were making the analysis to establish and determine what you are talking about, whether based on evidence of proof or any document. Apart from what you heard or read in the media?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: According to Jane's Infantry Weapons, barracks infantry weapons which is very -- is a database of small arms being used by the armies all over the world. You will see that every year preceding the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina and after the war, the M84 and M53 machine-guns will be mentioned in Yugoslavia or in the separate nations that were formed after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then it would mean that both parties had these kinds of weapons?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes. That is very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we can now go a little bit onwards, after the photographs on the next page, there is another piece of information, additional information. Page 20. I suppose it's the same in the English version? Here you say somewhere in the middle in the third passage: "The information provided by the victim determines the Grbavica area as the source of fire but this is contradictory to the coordinate mentioned in the witness report." You are making an assessment here which is contrary even to what the witness stated. Was that within your mandate as an expert?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'm trying to find it in the English. Can you help me find it, Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It's e-court page 20, yes, it's the very first line on the left-hand side. The information provided by the victim. Your Honour, there is a disjunct between the e-court page and the printed page. It is printed page 19 of 57 is e-court page 20 and it begins at the very top of -- the very top of the page. Exactly, Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it says here that the information provided by the victim determines the Grbavica area as the source of fire, but this is contradictory to the coordinate mentioned in the witness report? You are making an assessment here of what the witness said and you even recognise the existence of something that is contradictory.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That's true. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say: "This information indicates a location 50 metres east of the one given by the victim." Isn't that again something for this Trial Chamber to decide and assess?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The report reflected my personal opinion in my experience and with the information provided me -- to me by the Prosecutor and the visit -- my visiting Sarajevo and the incident site, I reached the conclusion that the victim -- the witness which in this case was also the victim, gave a location of -- mentions the Grbavica building as the source of fire, but the problem was that the location of the GPS coordinate which was provided from that coordinate it was not possible to see the Grbavica building so that is why I included this section in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you shifted it of all places to the Jewish cemetery which was known as a place of sniping activity. On the basis of what did you now suddenly decide that the location from which the shot came was the Jewish cemetery? Because it was a known place from which sniper fire came. How did you know that? Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I didn't conclude that Jewish cemetery was the origin of fire. And the Jewish cemetery was -- is mentioned in a different paragraph -- of in a different incident so -- that's why I included it in this case as well, from the Jewish cemetery it is possible to look to get a view of the incident site -- at the GPS coordinate, but for me it is -- for me it is more likely that the victim or the witness with the confusion happening at the time of the shooting mistook the exact moment when the shooting took place. You have to take into account that he is moving -- he is in a tram, that it is moving eastwards towards the town centre and -- well, according to the information -- to my summary, he suddenly hears shooting, saw people running, he recalled burst of fire. At that time before realising they are already several seconds farther into the incident and at that time the tram keeps moving, so I believe he was fired upon from the Grbavica building or at least a building marked in the -- in layout number 2, and the GPS coordinate was taken at the location where the tram stopped. So I didn't conclude that the firing came from -- originated from the Jewish Cemetery but, rather, from the Grbavica building or from Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us dwell a little bit longer what you say here, under heading additional information. Did the individuals who provided this additional information to you tell you that a significant part of the Jewish cemetery was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And at the end of this section, so last page relating to this incident, under the heading identification. I'd like to understand -- it's page 22 in B/C/S and I think it's the 21st or 22nd page in English. You can see it here, identification? What does this mean, what you said: "The previous incidents were widely reported on television and in newspapers since they happened under the nose of the international press assembled at Holiday Inn Hotel just metres away from the incident site"? What was the relevance of this, to your expert opinion of this whole incident? Did you succumb to the press -- through the pressure of the media?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No, I didn't. The reason why I included this under identification is as I have written a tram is a means of public transport. It is used to transport civilians. There were several -- according to my knowledge, and the information provided, there were several incidents in which trams were fired upon. I don't reach the conclusion as to which site shot at. I just indicate a direction from which -- where the shooter must have been. The incidents were almost all reported in -- by the international press at the Holiday Inn. It's just an indication that through the press coverage, the people shooting the weapons would have -- be able to conclude that there was civilians they were firing on and that should be, in my opinion, reason not to shoot at trams another time. So that is why I conclude this section in -- under identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to read to you the last paragraph where you speak again about the media. I'd like to ask you about your expert analysis. Could it have -- could anything that is written in the paper or published in the media have any bearing on your analysis, or was it your duty within the limits of your skills and the experience to establish what exactly happened?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It was my duty to -- to try to determine the source of fire, where the shooter might have been, what the range was, the most likely -- the weapon that was most likely used, an inside in sniping and also if it was possible to identify the victims or targets as combatant or non-combatant as referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can we just go briefly to incident 5 of the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English version 22, and B/C/S version page 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just for information, at this point I would have perhaps five minutes of re-direct of the Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take that into account, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I will finish by five to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here, you talk about an incident which took place on the 18th of November in which a little boy, Nerman Divovic, was killed. I'm not going to go into ballistic or sniper or any other elements with regard to this incident. What I would like to hear from you is to tell me this: How is it possible that even in this case, you didn't take into account the medical records? Can you explain that or not? Why didn't you use medical documentation in this case, either?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Medical documents weren't available to me, and I didn't deem them necessary for me to reach my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now case number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English page 25, B/C/S 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order to expedite my questioning, if you can see it, everything in relation to this case. Again, we have a tripod here, so do you maintain the same position as before with regard to a tripod for semi-automatic rifles M76 and M91.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I never concluded that the M76 or M91 were used on tripods since they are sniper rifles and they are not employed on tripods. If tripods -- if there are tripods mentioned, it is in conjunction with the M84 or 53 machine-gun, not with the M76 or M91 with sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The point here is that these semi-automatic rifles were most probably used; their accuracy is, again, within 50 metres?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No. That is not the case. I exclude the M70 assault rifle series because they are difficult to keep aimed at a target even at range under 50 metres. The reasons I -- in my opinion were used are the M84 and 53 machine-gun, bipod or tripod-mounted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But here you talk about semi-automatic sniper rifles M76 and M91. In what context was that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: They are in the context of being excluded because there were several shots fired at a rapid rate, which usually excludes sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that this is precisely characteristic of an exchange of fire between warring parties? I'm not going to tell you what happened on that particular day, it is for the Trial Chamber to examine this evidence, but isn't this characteristic of an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking of a tripod in general, do you know that this tripod for a machine-gun weighs 45 kilos? Who can carry that? If it is stationary, couldn't that become a target that can very easily and quickly be eliminated and annihilated? Do you know that it weighs 49 kilos?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I don't believe the tripod for the M84 weighs 45 kilos, but even if it weighs 45 kilos, a machine-gun or an urban shooting position can be reinforced with sandbags to keep it functioning for a longer time to make it sort of a bunker in a house. So it does -- a machine-gun does attract fire, as was evident by the bullet-holes visible -- still visible on the Grbavica building or the building that I visited. So, yes, I do believe it attracts fire, but it's not that easy to neutralise as a shooting position when using sandbags.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Incident number 13 and 14. Since it's the same story, I don't want to repeat it. But let us move on to incident number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] English page number 36; B/C/S, 40. I hope I will have enough time for that, too, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see the calibre, don't you? The use of hand-held launchers or anti-aircraft weapons, the range from which I believe the firing came is over 500 metres. My question is whether you know at all there are two types of hand-held launchers, if the maximum range is 240 metres - we heard about that from several witnesses here - do you know that at all? Do you know that on the basis of your own knowledge and experience?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It is on the basis of my own personal knowledge and experience, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And we have a few more incidents. Incident number 7 is the same, so I'm not going to dwell on that, and also the other tripods. But 10 and 15 are both incidents at Sedrenik. I would just like to ask you the following: You probably don't know that at all, that up there at Sedrenik, that you do not know at all where the separation lines were up there? You don't, right, at Spicasta Stijena? Or, rather, you mentioned Spicasta Stijena up here in your findings. Do you know that at Spicasta Stijena there were separation lines or, rather, where they were?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of any separation lines. I was aware that there are separation lines since there was a conflict. But I wasn't aware of any specific locations, apart from the positions visited by me which are visible on the -- I think that it's page 44 then, if it's in the English version, because I took the photo of trench lines that are still visible at the -- somewhere on that hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since there's no more time left, do you know that there, at Spicasta Stijena, most of the gun-fire exchanges occurred? I don't want to explain anything else to you now. Did anybody tell you that piece of information; that there was a great deal of fire exchange up there between the parties that were in conflict?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant, just a few questions in redirect. First of all, I want to clear up -- I'm a bit confused as to the role -- potential role of medical information in your analysis. Back at the beginning of cross-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic asked you a question about medical information, and I believe you said it could be important. And then towards the end of your cross-examination when being asked about the shooting of Nermin Divovic, you said that you did not have access to the medical information, and I believe you indicated it would not have mattered if you had, because it did not play a role in your analysis. And I'm just wondering if you could just clear up those two answers?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I will try to. The medical information -- every rifle round has different characteristics and will have a different effect when entering human tissue. If a witness states that he was hit by a 50-calibre round but in his knee -- but still has his knee, it will not have been a 50-calibre round because the 50-calibre round will probably -- will most likely destroy his -- completely and with it his lower leg. The problem that ballistic experts have with the police - and I know, I have had classes by ballistics experts - is most of the ballistic experts, the cases they handle take place within rooms or at short ranges in which -- under which you can use a dummy, insert sticks into the dummy to determine the exact origin of fire. The problem is at short ranges bullets travel in relatively straight lines, so with -- yeah, with a stick you could point back to the origin of fire, and that would help determining the type of weapon -- the origin of the shooting location. Coming back to medical information, it's standard military ammunition, as allowed by the Convention of Geneva, is full metal jacket, which doesn't have that much deformation when entering human tissue. It will tumble, it will cause damage, but it won't -- it will destroy tissue but not -- it won't destroy it that much. If you compare that to hunting ammunition, which is also available, hunting ammunition, especially the hollow-point ammunition, has a tendency to bloom open like a mushroom, which in a very short instance of time transfers kinetic energy towards -- to the body and destroying more of the tissue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Lieutenant, I'm sorry, maybe I could just cut short. I think -- perhaps we're miscommunicating. Let me ask you this: What role does medical information have if you're trying to determine the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: If you have the entry and exit wound of the victim and you have the exact body position and location of the victim, you would be able to get the -- the -- the direction of the shooter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Was the exact body location of the victim available to you in any of the cases that you studied in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: The exact body position was available, but the -- of the body location was available, but the body position was not available, apart from some testimony by the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And as a matter of an example, if someone is shot in the right side, let us say, does that information gain or lose usefulness depending upon whether the person was turning to their left, turning to their right, bending over, standing up straight, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Moving quickly to this question of muzzle climb that took quite awhile on cross-examination. When -- start with this proposition: When a gun is fired, it recoils; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And just to get some terminology, what does it mean when you say that a weapon is being fired on full automatic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: On full automatic, when -- keeping the trigger depressed, when pressing the trigger the bullets will -- the whole action of the weapon will automatically cycle and keep going automatic firing bullets until the trigger is released.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And with the weapons that are used in NATO armies, when a weapon, an assault rifle, is being fired on full automatic, about how many rounds a minute are coming out of the barrel, as an approximation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I would say seven to 800 rounds a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this recoil that you mentioned a few -- a minute or two ago, what does that do to the barrel of the rifle every time that a round leaves it? Does it move it up, down, left, right, or what?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It depends upon the design of the weapon, but in general the weapon goes up and to the right -- the barrel to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when a weapon is being fired on full automatic, and this is happening is seven to 800 times per minute, how much control does the rifleman have over this motion upwards and to the right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: If it is an assault rifle used on automatic from standing or a sitting position, he has very limited control. To give an impression, at 5 metres firing an automatic weapon, it would probably -- the first round would hit at the target, but the second round would probably hit 10 centimetres up and to the right, and so on and so on. So within five shots, it will be off the target at 5 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And is this the phenomenon that you call muzzle climb?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: How much of a factor is muzzle climb when you are firing not on fully automatic but on semi-automatic, or even single-firing with a bolt-action rifle?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Muzzle climb still happens, but it is not of importance because every -- with every shot fired on semi-automatic or single shot, the shooter will come back with his rifle in the direction where he -- on his target, get his target in his sight, and will then press the trigger another time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then lastly, Lieutenant, there was lot of testimony concerning this incident number 2, the shooting of the young man through the tunnel, and I'm not going to draw triangles and I'm not going to -- or anything like that. But you were at the scene; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And looked through that tunnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. You are a fairly good shot, would you say?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: I would say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. And, Lieutenant, if you were to take that shot, from the highest point in those buildings that are outlined in your report, if you were going take that shot ten times, about how many times do you think you would hit the target?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK VAN DER WEIJDEN
utterances.text: If there would be a paper target at that location stationary, I would hit it ten times easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant. That concludes your testimony. Thank you for giving it, and you may now leave. Please escort the Lieutenant out. I have an administrative matter to attend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As a result of the joint motion filed by the Prosecution and the Defence to amend the Scheduling Order of the 15th of March, the Chamber has decided to amend its order, and I will now give you the new dates. I should say immediately that the Chamber will have a written decision filed. The Trial Chamber will sit from 9.00 until 5:00 on Friday, the 20th of April and the 27th as well, provided that a courtroom will be available in the afternoon. That is for the 27th, and that is to be confirmed as soon as possible. The Prosecution case will close on Wednesday, the 2nd of May. Oral submissions of both parties pursuant to Rule 98 bis, if any, will be made on Thursday, the 3rd of May. The submissions pursuant to that Rule are to be made within a time frame of one and a half hours for each party, and the decision, in relation to that submission, will be rendered on Thursday, the 3rd of May. The Defence is to provide the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber with a list of their first two witnesses and the 65 ter summaries for those witnesses on Tuesday, the 15th of May. The Defence will file their submissions pursuant to Rule 65 ter on Monday, the 21st of May by 1.00 p.m. at the latest. The pre-Defence conference will take place on Thursday, the 24th of May, and will last no longer than one and a half hours. The pre-Defence conference will be immediately followed by the Defence opening statement, which will last no longer than one and a half hours. The first witness for the Defence will be heard on Thursday, the 24th of May, following the Defence opening statement. The Trial Chamber will not sit on Friday, the 25th of the May.
